ap_statistics-m01.stem: The histogram shown summarizes the time, in minutes, that each of $54$ customers spent waiting in line at a bank. In which class does the median time lie?

options.why: The $54$ observations put the median at position $27$ and $28$; adding the bar heights from the left, the running total first reaches that position in this class.
Picks the class where the cumulative count reaches three quarters of the data, which is the third quartile, not the median.
Picks the middle class of the horizontal axis rather than locating the position of the median from cumulative counts.
Picks the tallest bar (the modal class) instead of the class where half of the observations have been accumulated.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Locate the median class of a distribution displayed in a histogram
student_thinking: Read each bar height and add them to find the number of observations
Find the position of the median and the class where the running total of frequencies first reaches it

key_conditions.condition: the median of grouped data lies in the class where the cumulative frequency first reaches the median position
key_conditions.evidence: the classes have equal width and each bar height is the class frequency

misconceptions.description: picks the tallest bar as the median class
picks the middle class of the axis
reports the class of the first or third quartile

verification.independent_path: the data are expanded into a sorted list using class midpoints and the median is taken with numpy, independent of the cumulative-count rule

ap_statistics-m02.stem: The boxplot shown summarizes the lengths of phone calls, in minutes, at a call center. The first quartile is $15$ and the third quartile is $25$. According to the $1.5\times \mathrm{IQR}$ rule, a value above what boundary is classified as a high outlier?

stimulus.description: Boxplot of lengths of phone calls

options.why: IQR $= 25 - 15 = 10$, so the boundary is $Q_3 + 1.5\times \mathrm{IQR} = 25 + 15 = 40$.
Computes the lower boundary $Q_1 - 1.5\times \mathrm{IQR}$, which is used for low outliers, not high ones.
Reports 1.5 times the IQR without adding it to the third quartile.
Adds one IQR to the third quartile instead of 1.5 times the IQR.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Apply the 1.5 IQR rule to find the boundary for high outliers shown on a boxplot
student_thinking: Find the interquartile range from the given quartiles
Apply the 1.5 times IQR rule above the third quartile and decide which boundary applies to high outliers

key_conditions.condition: a value is a high outlier when it exceeds Q3 + 1.5 IQR
key_conditions.evidence: the boxplot marks the one observation beyond this boundary with a dot while the whisker stops at the largest non-outlier

verification.independent_path: candidate values at the boundary plus and minus 0.01 are tested against the rule with exact fractions, and the plotted whisker end and outlier are checked to lie below and above the boundary

ap_statistics-m03.stem: On Test A, which has mean $76$ and standard deviation $4$, a student scored $81$. On Test B, which has mean $79$ and standard deviation $8$, the same student scored $85$. On which test did the student perform better relative to the other test takers?

options.text: Test B, because the raw score of $85$ is greater than the raw score of $81$ on Test A
options.why: Compares raw scores from two tests that have different means and standard deviations.

options.text: Test A, because its z-score of $1.25$ is greater than the z-score of $0.75$ on Test B
options.why: The z-scores are $z_A = (81-76)/4 = 1.25$ and $z_B = (85-79)/8 = 0.75$; the larger z-score marks the better relative performance.

options.text: Neither test, because the tests have different standard deviations and cannot be compared
options.why: Believes scores on different scales can never be compared even though z-scores put them on a common scale.

options.text: Test B, because the score is $6$ points above the mean, more than $5$ points on Test A
options.why: Compares distances from the mean in points instead of in standard deviations.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Compare relative standing on two tests using z-scores
student_thinking: Standardize each score using its own test mean and standard deviation
Compare the z-scores to decide relative performance

key_conditions.condition: relative position on different scales is compared with z-scores
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the mean and standard deviation of each test

misconceptions.description: compares distance from the mean in points

verification.independent_path: normal percentile ranks from scipy.stats.norm.cdf are compared and must order the tests exactly as the z-scores do

ap_statistics-m04.stem: The table shown summarizes the responses of $230$ patients. One patient is selected at random. Given that the patient improved, what is the probability that the patient was treated at the North clinic? Round to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: Two-way table of clinic and response

options.why: Divides by the grand total, which gives the probability of both events instead of the conditional probability.
Given the column, the total is $106$ and $49$ of them are in the row: $49/106 \approx 0.462$.
Divides by the row total instead of the column total, which reverses the condition.
Reports the overall proportion in the row, ignoring the given information.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Compute a conditional probability from a two-way table
student_thinking: Restrict attention to the group named by the given condition (one column)
Divide the count of the event within that group by the group total, not by the grand total or the row total

key_conditions.condition: P(A given B) divides the joint count by the total for B
key_conditions.evidence: the table gives all counts and the stem names the given condition

verification.independent_path: every respondent is expanded into an individual record and the conditional proportion is found by enumeration, independent of the cell-count ratio

ap_statistics-m05.stem: At an electronics assembler, each part comes from Supplier A or Supplier B, as shown in the tree diagram. One part is selected at random and is faulty. What is the probability that the part came from Supplier A? Round to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: Probability tree for Supplier and outcome

options.why: $P(\text{A}\mid \text{faulty}) = 0.0450/0.0750 \approx 0.600$: the branch for A then faulty, divided by the total probability of faulty.
Reports the overall probability of being faulty, not the probability of A given that.
Reports the probability of A and faulty together, without dividing by the probability of being faulty.
Reports the probability of being faulty given A, which reverses the conditional probability asked for.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Reverse a conditional probability using a probability tree
student_thinking: Compute the probability of each path ending in the given outcome
Divide the path through the named source by the total probability of the outcome

key_conditions.condition: P(source given outcome) = P(source and outcome) / P(outcome)
key_conditions.evidence: the tree gives the source probabilities and the conditional outcome probabilities on each branch

verification.independent_path: a population of 100000 items is built from the tree with integer counts per path and the conditional proportion is computed from the counts

ap_statistics-m06.stem: A basketball player attempts $15$ free throws, each of which is independently made with probability $0.4$. What is the probability that exactly $7$ of the free throws are made? Round to three decimal places.

options.why: With $15$ independent trials and constant probability, $X$ is binomial: $P(X=7) = \binom{15}{7}(0.4)^{7}(0.6)^{8} \approx 0.177$.
Finds the probability of at most $7$ successes instead of exactly $7$.
Swaps the success and failure probabilities.
Finds the probability of fewer than $7$ successes instead of exactly $7$.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Recognize a binomial setting and find the probability of exactly k successes
student_thinking: Check that the trials are independent with a fixed number and a constant probability of success so that the count is binomial
Evaluate the probability of exactly k successes rather than a cumulative probability

key_conditions.condition: the count of successes is binomial when n is fixed, trials are independent and p is constant
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states each trial is independent with the same probability

verification.independent_path: the probability is recomputed with math.comb and powers directly, independent of scipy.stats.binom

ap_statistics-m07.stem: The lengths of fish in a lake, in centimeters, are approximately normally distributed with mean $43.75$ and standard deviation $3.5$. The curve shown has the area to the right of $46.55$ shaded. Approximately what proportion of the fish have a value greater than $46.55$? Round to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: Normal curve with the area to the right of 46.55 shaded

options.why: $z = (46.55-43.75)/3.5 = 0.8$ and the area to the right of $z$ is about $0.212$.
Doubles the tail area as if the question asked about values far from the mean in either direction.
Divides the distance from the mean by the variance instead of the standard deviation when finding the z-score.
Uses the area to the left of the value instead of the area to the right.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Find the proportion of a normal population above a value
student_thinking: Standardize the value using the mean and the standard deviation
Find the area in the upper tail of the standard normal distribution

key_conditions.condition: the proportion above x equals the upper-tail area at z = (x - mean)/sd
key_conditions.evidence: the stem says the distribution is approximately normal and gives the mean and standard deviation

verification.independent_path: the upper-tail area is computed from math.erf, independent of scipy.stats.norm.sf, and the plotted curve is a density with unit area

ap_statistics-m08.stem: A company states that $0.6$ of its customers renew a subscription. In a random sample of $200$ customers, $132$ renewed. A test of $H_0: p = 0.6$ versus $H_a: p \ne 0.6$ is conducted, and the conditions for inference are met. Which gives the test statistic and the P-value? Round $z$ to two decimal places and the P-value to three decimal places.

options.why: Reports the area on the wrong side of the test statistic as the P-value.
Uses the wrong number of tails for the alternative hypothesis when finding the P-value.
Uses the sample proportion rather than the hypothesized proportion in the standard error of the test statistic.
$z = (0.660-0.6)/\sqrt{0.6(0.4)/200} \approx 1.73$ using the hypothesized proportion in the standard error, and the P-value is the matching normal tail area.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Carry out a one-sample z test for a proportion
student_thinking: Compute the standard error from the hypothesized proportion and standardize the sample proportion
Find the P-value from the normal tail area that matches the alternative hypothesis

key_conditions.condition: a one-proportion z test uses the hypothesized proportion in the standard error
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states the null value, the alternative and that the conditions are met

misconceptions.description: puts p-hat in the standard error
uses the wrong number of tails

verification.independent_path: the P-value is recomputed from math.erf rather than scipy.stats.norm and every wrong option is checked to round to a different pair of values

ap_statistics-m09.stem: A bakery claims that its loaves have a mean mass of $50$ grams. A random sample of $9$ loaves has a mean mass of $51.2$ grams and a standard deviation of $2.1$ grams, and the conditions for inference are met. A test of $H_0: \mu = 50$ versus $H_a: \mu \ne 50$ is conducted. The t distribution curve shown has the area that corresponds to the P-value shaded. Which gives the test statistic and the P-value? Round $t$ to two decimal places and the P-value to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: t distribution with 8 degrees of freedom; the shaded area is the P-value region

options.why: Divides the sample standard deviation by the square root of $n-1$ instead of the square root of $n$.
Finds the P-value from the standard normal distribution instead of the t distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
$t = (51.2-50)/(2.1/\sqrt{9}) \approx 1.71$ with $8$ degrees of freedom, and the P-value is the matching tail area of the t distribution.
Uses the wrong number of tails for the alternative hypothesis when finding the P-value.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Carry out a one-sample t test for a mean
student_thinking: Standardize the sample mean with the standard error s divided by the square root of n
Find the P-value from the t distribution with n minus 1 degrees of freedom and the tail count that matches the alternative

key_conditions.condition: a one-sample t test uses s over the square root of n and a t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the sample statistics, the null value, the alternative and that conditions are met

misconceptions.description: divides by the square root of n - 1
uses the wrong number of tails

verification.independent_path: the t tail area is obtained by numerically integrating the t density with scipy.integrate.quad, independent of scipy.stats.t

ap_statistics-m10.stem: A researcher compares two study methods using independent random samples; the summary statistics for the test score (in points) are shown. Assuming the conditions for inference are met, which is a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, where group 1 is Method 1 and group 2 is Method 2? Round the endpoints to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: Summary statistics for two study methods

options.why: Uses the standard normal critical value instead of a t critical value, which makes the interval too narrow.
Adds the two standard errors instead of combining the variances under a square root.
Finds the interval for the difference in the opposite order, $\mu_2 - \mu_1$.
The standard error is $\sqrt{5.7^2/15+3.8^2/16} \approx 1.752$, the degrees of freedom are about $24.2$, and $t^* \approx 2.063$ for $95\%$ confidence.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Construct a two-sample t interval for a difference of means from summary statistics
student_thinking: Combine the two sample variances under one square root for the standard error and use the t critical value for the approximate degrees of freedom
Choose the interval that matches the order of subtraction stated in the question

key_conditions.condition: a two-sample t interval uses the unpooled standard error and a t critical value
key_conditions.evidence: the table gives each sample size, mean and standard deviation and the stem states the order of subtraction

verification.independent_path: scipy.stats.ttest_ind_from_stats confidence_interval reproduces the endpoints and the t critical value is found by inverting the numerically integrated t cdf
